title: Iron and the female athlete: a review of dietary treatment methods for improving iron status and exercise performance
publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
claims: Iron absorption has an inverse relationship with serum ferritin up to about 60 micrograms per litre; at a ferritin of 10 micrograms per litre, absorption of both haem and non-haem iron was about 40%, and absorption fell at higher ferritin levels, especially for non-haem iron.

Haem iron absorption can be as efficient as 40%, non-haem iron absorption varies from 2% to 20%, haem iron is only about 10% of all dietary iron, and about 50% of dietary iron in Western diets comes from grain products.
Iron deficiency progresses in three stages: storage depletion, reduced erythropoiesis with low transport iron, and anaemia when haemoglobin synthesis falls.

The physiological serum ferritin range in adult females is 15 to 200 micrograms per litre; the lower limit used to define latent iron deficiency in physically active females varies from 12 to 35 micrograms per litre, and 12 micrograms per litre generally indicates absent bone-marrow iron stores.
Pate et al. found that 50% of 111 distance runners had serum ferritin below 20 micrograms per litre; Koehler et al. found that 57% of 97 athletes had a value below 35 micrograms per litre.

The UK reference nutrient intake for adult females is 14.8 mg iron per day and the US recommended dietary allowance is 18 mg per day; some authors suggest endurance female athletes, especially distance runners, need about 70% more iron, which would add roughly 10 mg per day to the UK value.

In one study, vegetarian runners had a significantly lower serum ferritin (7.4 micrograms per litre) than meat eaters (19.8 micrograms per litre) despite similar total iron intake, with absorbable iron of 0.66 versus 0.91 mg per day.
